analysis.one_liner: Freezes federal air pollution standards at existing levels, barring EPA from strengthening them.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, died in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have locked every national air quality standard in place as of the day it was signed, and barred the EPA from revising an existing standard or issuing a new one. Under the Clean Air Act, EPA currently reviews and updates these standards as health science advances; this bill would have made any change require a new act of Congress. It was named the Manufacturers First Act because the main beneficiaries would be factories and other emitters that avoid the cost of meeting tighter standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers, power plants, and other industrial emitters would gain the most: pollution standards could never be tightened by regulators, so compliance costs would stay frozen no matter what new health research showed. The CRS summary notes the bill stops EPA from issuing, implementing, or enforcing any revision to existing health-based and welfare-based air standards or any new standard, except when Congress itself passes a statute [S2][S3]. Industry would get long-term regulatory certainty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Factories and other industrial air emitters

how_it_helps.text: Freezes all national primary (public health) and secondary (public welfare) air quality standards at their levels on the bill's enactment date, so no standard could be strengthened by the executive branch.
Gives manufacturers and other emitters certainty that the cost of complying with air pollution limits will not rise, since only a new act of Congress could change a standard.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the health cost. Primary air quality standards exist specifically to protect public health from pollutants like ozone and particulate matter, and the bill would prevent them from being updated even if evidence showed current pollution levels are unsafe [S2]. People living near highways, industrial facilities, and other pollution sources — along with children, the elderly, and people with asthma and heart or lung disease — would be exposed to whatever pollution levels 2015 science deemed acceptable, indefinitely.
analysis.who_pays_short: People breathing polluted air, especially asthma sufferers

drawbacks.text: Air quality standards could never be strengthened, even if new research showed that current pollution limits are harming people's health — the standards the bill freezes are the ones designed to protect public health.
Moving standard-setting from EPA scientists' ongoing reviews to one-off acts of Congress is slow and politically fraught, so protections would likely go stale rather than being deliberately updated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: industry gains cost certainty and avoids spending on pollution controls that stricter standards would require. The cost is diffuse but serious: public health protection would be permanently frozen at mid-2010s levels, with no mechanism to tighten standards as the science on air pollution evolves, and updating them through Congress for each pollutant would be slow and unlikely. On balance, the bill shifts costs from a concentrated set of emitters to the general public's health.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, not even a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman introduced the bill on June 16, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it stayed; no further action was ever taken.
Not a single member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people and public health came out ahead: EPA's authority to review and strengthen air quality standards as science advanced was left intact because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health; EPA kept its clean-air authority

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his sole sponsorship; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Power
against.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 19, 2015 and never scheduled a hearing or vote; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsor was a Republican and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other industrial air emitters
industries.note: With standards frozen, factories would never face tighter limits on the pollution they release, avoiding compliance costs indefinitely. That saving comes directly out of the air quality of people living near those facilities.
Power plants are among the largest sources of the pollutants covered by national air standards; freezing the standards would spare them costly upgrades to scrubbers and other controls.

industries.industry: Pollution-control and air monitoring equipment makers
industries.note: Demand for scrubbers, filters, and monitoring equipment grows when standards tighten; a permanent freeze would take away that growth. Their interest runs alongside the public's interest in cleaner air.
